 French Government Announces Minimum Wage Increase and Tax Relief for Employers
 France Minimum Wage France raises minimum wage 1.6 percent early Increase moves up to 1 December Pay talks continue across sectors Loading Stock video by Kiwi and Camera via Pexels 
 Nov 9, 2026 
 French Government Announces Minimum Wage Increase and Tax Relief for Employers
 Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu unveiled a set of measures aimed at easing social discontent while addressing employer concerns, according to Euronews . Speaking after a Monday morning conference at Matignon with representatives of employees and employers, the head of government outlined steps intended to boost purchasing power and encourage wage growth. 
 The central measure is a 1.6 percent increase in the minimum wage, brought forward to 1 December from the previously planned 1 January 2027. The change will lift the minimum wage to roughly 1,502 euros net per month, a gain of 24 euros net monthly. A decree is expected to be published shortly, and Lecornu described the move as the second largest increase in the past two decades.
 Lecornu argued that raising the minimum wage alone is insufficient but carries an important benefit by opening a cycle of discussions on pay increases. He also announced the launch of a reform project on general reductions in social security contributions, intended to raise the net salary employees receive.
 Asked at a press conference about the time the government was perceived to have wasted before responding, Lecornu defended his approach, saying he no longer believes in headline-grabbing announcements and considers them harmful. He said he wants to present measures that work when appearing before the French public, adding that the government is doing everything it can and favoring concrete steps over rushed announcements.
 Tax Measures Aimed at Businesses
 To address business concerns about rising labor costs, the government plans parallel tax measures: income tax exemption for overtime up to 10,000 euros, exemption of employer contributions to public transport costs, and making value-sharing bonuses tax free. The value-sharing bonus, sometimes called the Macron bonus, lets companies pay employees a one-off sum to redistribute part of the value created, with favorable tax and social security treatment under certain conditions.
 Lecornu summarized that several chapters had been opened with detailed proposals, and he now intends for the state to act as guarantor of mutual commitments between employees and employers. Negotiations are to continue across roughly one hundred professional sectors, each of which will need to discuss its own arrangements for increasing pay. Lecornu stressed the need for sincere commitments, contrasting them with promises he sees multiplying as the presidential election approaches, and said the government, which has no electoral timetable, has a duty to find solutions.
 Union Reaction
 Initial union reaction remains cautious. The 1.6 percent minimum wage increase falls well short of their original demands, with the CFDT seeking an additional 100 euros net per month and the CGT around 150 euros. Before the announcements, CFTC president Cyril Chabanier had already said the measures under consideration were not commensurate with the level of social anger. The CGT, through general secretary Sophie Binet, is calling for another major day of strikes and demonstrations on 17 November.
